newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanians choose between ex-communist or reformer.
newsitem.headline: Romanians choose between ex-communist or reformer.

text.p: Romanians trudged out to vote on Sunday in a presidential election that could end the long political dominance of ex-communists in the Balkan country.

Reformist Emil Constantinescu is locked in a tight run-off fight against Ion Iliescu, a former communist who has ruled for the nearly seven years since Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was ousted and executed.

More than 15,000 polling stations in schools and village halls across the impoverished country opened in light mist at 6 a.m. (0400 GMT). The elderly, wanting to avoid a crush later in the day, formed the first trickle of voters.
"I came early to be done with it," pensioner Dobre Dan, 67, said outside a Bucharest polling station. "I voted for Constantinescu. I want all this misery to end."

Voting in rural areas, once Iliescu's bedrock of support, was slower as people attended church services before heading off to polling stations. The president needs a heavy turnout in these areas to have any hope of staying in office.
Constantinescu, needing to impress peasants and pensioners, was due to pray at an Orthodox monastery before voting.
Exit polls will give the first indication of the result shortly after the last vote is cast at midnight (2200 gmt). Official results will trickle in throughout Monday.
Unlike Iliescu, tainted by holding high office under Ceausescu and accused of ruling in an arrogant and demagogic manner, Constantinescu held no position under communism.
He pledges a new era of clean government, better economic management and reforms to stop living standards in Romania lagging further behind ex-communist near neighbours like Hungary and Poland.
The mild-mannered geology professor charges Iliescu led a corrupt, incompetent administration that failed to remedy Romania's fiscal woes and crumbling infrastructure.

He has taken heart from the first round of voting two weeks ago when Romanians, fed up with eking out a living on salaries of some $100 a month, ousted Iliescu's leftist party from government and installed Constantinescu's reform group.
In bitter television debates, Iliescu has played on the conservatism and fears of many Romanians and said a victory for him would protect people from the costs of social change.

"I am convinced voters will understand that to preserve national unity and peace for coming generations they must vote for Iliescu," said Adrian Nastase, leader of Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy.
There have been no reliable opinion polls since the first round and the contest is thought too close to call.
Town dwellers and the young are expected to back the challenger's vision of reform while pensioners and rural voters may plump for Iliescu's message of caution.
"I expect the president to improve the situation," said Maglasu Aurelia, 70. "I voted for Iliescu."
But Constantinescu may benefit from disillusion with the negative campaigning style of the 66-year-old president, who has reportedly been worn out by the election struggle.

First round voting was marked by confusion over outdated votes list, with thousands having to register on "additional lists". But international observers pronounced the ballot generally free and fair.
